title: Meet your customers
statement: A good analysis starts with the people. Return the id, name and city of every customer, in that column order. No particular row order is required.
solution: SELECT id, name, city FROM customers
hints: Start with the customers table.
SELECT chooses columns; FROM chooses a table.
List id, name and city after SELECT, separated by commas.

title: Hello, Bengaluru
statement: Return id and name for customers whose city is Bengaluru.
solution: SELECT id,name FROM customers WHERE city='Bengaluru'
hints: Keep only one city.
Use WHERE with an equality comparison.
Text values need single quotes: city = 'Bengaluru'.

title: The missing addresses
statement: Return id and name of customers without an email address.
solution: SELECT id,name FROM customers WHERE email IS NULL
hints: A missing value is NULL.
NULL is not equal to anything, even another NULL.
Use email IS NULL, not email = NULL.

title: The sweet spot
statement: Return name and price of products priced from 25 through 65 inclusive.
solution: SELECT name,price FROM products WHERE price BETWEEN 25 AND 65
hints: Filter the products table.
Both endpoints should be included.
BETWEEN 25 AND 65 includes 25 and 65.

title: Where we call home
statement: Return each distinct non-null customer city once.
solution: SELECT DISTINCT city FROM customers WHERE city IS NOT NULL
hints: Cities appear more than once.
DISTINCT removes duplicate rows.
Filter NULL using IS NOT NULL.

title: Top shelf
statement: Return id, name and price of the three most expensive products. Sort by price descending, breaking ties by id ascending.
solution: SELECT id,name,price FROM products ORDER BY price DESC,id ASC LIMIT 3
hints: Sort before limiting.
DESC puts the highest price first.
Use ORDER BY price DESC, id ASC and LIMIT 3.

title: Fresh faces
statement: Return id, name and joined_at for the five newest customers, newest date first and id ascending for ties.
solution: SELECT id,name,joined_at FROM customers ORDER BY joined_at DESC,id LIMIT 5
hints: Dates are ISO text.
Sort joined_at descending.
Add id as a tie-breaker, then LIMIT 5.

title: A busy little shop
statement: Return a single value: the total number of orders, including cancelled orders.
solution: SELECT COUNT(*) FROM orders
hints: You need one summary row.
COUNT counts rows.
COUNT(*) includes rows with missing values.

title: A price check
statement: Return the average product price rounded to two decimal places.
solution: SELECT ROUND(AVG(price),2) FROM products
hints: Use an aggregate over products.
AVG calculates the mean.
Wrap AVG(price) in ROUND(..., 2).

title: On the shelves
statement: Return the total number of units in stock across all products.
solution: SELECT SUM(stock) FROM products
hints: Count units, not products.
SUM adds a numeric column.
Sum the stock column in products.

title: Loud and clear
statement: Return id and the uppercase customer name for every customer.
solution: SELECT id,UPPER(name) FROM customers
hints: Keep the id unchanged.
SQLite has UPPER for uppercase text.
Use UPPER(name) as the second column.

title: The class of 2024
statement: Return id and name of customers who joined during calendar year 2024.
solution: SELECT id,name FROM customers WHERE strftime('%Y',joined_at)='2024'
hints: joined_at is an ISO date string.
strftime can extract a date part.
strftime('%Y', joined_at) returns the year as text.

title: In stock or not?
statement: Return name and a label: 'Sold out' when stock is zero, otherwise 'Available'.
solution: SELECT name,CASE WHEN stock=0 THEN 'Sold out' ELSE 'Available' END FROM products
hints: Each product needs one of two labels.
Use CASE WHEN ... THEN ... ELSE ... END.
Test stock = 0 and return the exact labels in the prompt.

title: No city, no problem
statement: Return id and city for all customers, replacing a missing city with 'Unknown'.
solution: SELECT id,COALESCE(city,'Unknown') FROM customers
hints: Only replace NULL, not other cities.
COALESCE chooses the first non-null argument.
Use COALESCE(city, 'Unknown').

title: A map of our customers
statement: Return city and customer count for each non-null city.
solution: SELECT city,COUNT(*) FROM customers WHERE city IS NOT NULL GROUP BY city
hints: Group customers by city.
Filter NULL before grouping.
SELECT city, COUNT(*) with GROUP BY city.

title: Our busiest cities
statement: Return city and customer count for non-null cities with at least three customers.
solution: SELECT city,COUNT(*) FROM customers WHERE city IS NOT NULL GROUP BY city HAVING COUNT(*)>=3
hints: Start with counts per city.
HAVING filters whole groups.
Use HAVING COUNT(*) >= 3 after GROUP BY.

title: Compare the shelves
statement: Return category_id and average price rounded to two decimals for products with a non-null category_id, one row per category_id.
solution: SELECT category_id,ROUND(AVG(price),2) FROM products WHERE category_id IS NOT NULL GROUP BY category_id
hints: Group by category_id.
Remove uncategorised products first.
Round the group average to two decimals.

title: A year in orders
statement: Return month as YYYY-MM and order count for every month represented in orders. Include all statuses. Sort month ascending.
solution: SELECT strftime('%Y-%m',ordered_at),COUNT(*) FROM orders GROUP BY strftime('%Y-%m',ordered_at) ORDER BY 1
hints: Extract year and month together.
strftime('%Y-%m', ordered_at) gives a sortable month.
Group by that expression and order by the first column.

title: Put a name to an order
statement: Return order id and customer name for orders with a matching customer. Include every status.
solution: SELECT o.id,c.name FROM orders o INNER JOIN customers c ON c.id=o.customer_id
hints: orders stores a customer_id.
An INNER JOIN keeps matching rows.
Match c.id = o.customer_id.

title: Still just browsing
statement: Return customer id and name for customers who have never placed an order.
solution: SELECT c.id,c.name FROM customers c LEFT JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id=c.id WHERE o.id IS NULL
hints: Keep customers even without matches.
A LEFT JOIN produces NULL order fields for unmatched customers.
Filter WHERE o.id IS NULL after the join.

title: Every team counts
statement: Using a RIGHT JOIN, return each department name and number of assigned employees. Include departments with zero employees. (The checker compares results, not syntax.)
solution: SELECT d.name,COUNT(e.id) FROM employees e RIGHT JOIN departments d ON e.department_id=d.id GROUP BY d.id,d.name
hints: Keep every department on the right.
RIGHT JOIN is supported by modern SQLite (3.39+).
Count e.id rather than * so empty departments count as zero.

title: Nobody left behind
statement: Return employee name and department name for all employees and all departments, including unassigned employees and empty departments. Practice FULL OUTER JOIN; unmatched names should be NULL.
solution: SELECT e.name,d.name FROM employees e FULL OUTER JOIN departments d ON e.department_id=d.id
hints: Keep unmatched rows from both sides.
Use a FULL OUTER JOIN (SQLite 3.39+).
Join employees.department_id to departments.id.

title: Meet the managers
statement: Return each employee name and their manager name. Include employees with no manager as NULL in the second column.
solution: SELECT e.name,m.name FROM employees e LEFT JOIN employees m ON e.manager_id=m.id
hints: Both people live in employees.
Join the table to itself using two aliases.
LEFT JOIN employees m ON e.manager_id = m.id.

title: A planning grid
statement: Return every combination of category name and distinct non-null customer city, once per pair. Practice a CROSS JOIN.
solution: SELECT c.name,x.city FROM categories c CROSS JOIN (SELECT DISTINCT city FROM customers WHERE city IS NOT NULL) x
hints: This is a Cartesian product.
Prepare the unique non-null cities in a subquery.
CROSS JOIN categories to that subquery.

title: A little above average
statement: Return id, name and price of products whose price exceeds the overall average product price.
solution: SELECT id,name,price FROM products WHERE price>(SELECT AVG(price) FROM products)
hints: Compute the overall average separately.
A scalar subquery can appear in WHERE.
Compare price > (SELECT AVG(price) FROM products).

title: Waiting for a first sale
statement: Return id and name of products that never appear in order_items, regardless of order status.
solution: SELECT p.id,p.name FROM products p WHERE NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM order_items i WHERE i.product_id=p.id)
hints: Test for the absence of an item.
NOT EXISTS avoids the NULL pitfalls of NOT IN.
Correlate i.product_id with the outer p.id.

title: Something for every budget
statement: Return name and a price band: 'Budget' below 30, 'Mid-range' from 30 up to but not including 100, and 'Premium' at 100 or more.
solution: SELECT name,CASE WHEN price<30 THEN 'Budget' WHEN price<100 THEN 'Mid-range' ELSE 'Premium' END FROM products
hints: CASE picks the first matching condition.
Test the lowest threshold first.
Use two WHEN conditions and a final ELSE.

title: How long did it take?
statement: For orders with shipped_at present, return order id and whole days between ordered_at and shipped_at.
solution: SELECT id,CAST(julianday(shipped_at)-julianday(ordered_at) AS INTEGER) FROM orders WHERE shipped_at IS NOT NULL
hints: Do not subtract date strings directly.
julianday converts a date to a day number.
Subtract the two julianday values and cast as INTEGER.

title: Read the receipt
statement: Return order_id and net order total rounded to two decimals from order_items. Net item value is quantity × unit_price × (1 − discount). Include all statuses.
solution: SELECT order_id,ROUND(SUM(quantity*unit_price*(1-discount)),2) FROM order_items GROUP BY order_id
hints: Discount is a fraction such as 0.1.
Sum net line values per order.
Round after summing, not before.

title: The 500 club
statement: Return customer_id and net spend rounded to two decimals for customers whose delivered-order spend exceeds 500. Exclude NULL customer_id. Net value is quantity × unit_price × (1 − discount).
solution: SELECT o.customer_id,ROUND(SUM(i.quantity*i.unit_price*(1-i.discount)),2) FROM orders o JOIN order_items i ON i.order_id=o.id WHERE o.status='delivered' AND o.customer_id IS NOT NULL GROUP BY o.customer_id HAVING SUM(i.quantity*i.unit_price*(1-i.discount))>500
hints: Join orders to their items.
Filter delivered orders before grouping by customer.
Use HAVING on the unrounded sum, then round the output.

title: Make it readable
statement: Using a CTE for order totals, return order id and net total for orders with net total above 200, rounded to two decimals. Include all statuses. Net value is quantity × unit_price × (1 − discount).
solution: WITH totals AS (SELECT order_id,SUM(quantity*unit_price*(1-discount)) AS total FROM order_items GROUP BY order_id) SELECT order_id,ROUND(total,2) FROM totals WHERE total>200
hints: Name the order-total calculation with WITH.
Group items by order_id inside the CTE.
Filter total > 200 in the outer SELECT.

title: Ahead of the team
statement: Return id, name and salary of employees earning more than the average salary in their own department. Exclude unassigned employees.
solution: SELECT e.id,e.name,e.salary FROM employees e WHERE e.department_id IS NOT NULL AND e.salary>(SELECT AVG(x.salary) FROM employees x WHERE x.department_id=e.department_id)
hints: Each employee needs a department-specific average.
A correlated subquery can use the outer department_id.
Compare salary to AVG(salary) for that same department.

title: A fair ranking
statement: Return employee id, department_id, salary and a dense salary rank within each department. Exclude unassigned employees. Highest salary has rank 1; ties share a rank with no gaps.
solution: SELECT id,department_id,salary,DENSE_RANK() OVER(PARTITION BY department_id ORDER BY salary DESC) FROM employees WHERE department_id IS NOT NULL
hints: A window preserves each employee row.
Partition by department_id.
DENSE_RANK with salary DESC gives tied ranks without gaps.

title: Watch the total grow
statement: Return order id, ordered_at and cumulative net value over all orders, sorted by ordered_at then order id ascending. Include all statuses. Compute each order's net value first; round only the final cumulative output to two decimals.
solution: WITH t AS (SELECT o.id,o.ordered_at,SUM(i.quantity*i.unit_price*(1-i.discount)) AS total FROM orders o JOIN order_items i ON i.order_id=o.id GROUP BY o.id,o.ordered_at) SELECT id,ordered_at,ROUND(SUM(total) OVER(ORDER BY ordered_at,id ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW),2) FROM t ORDER BY ordered_at,id
hints: First reduce the items to one row per order.
Use SUM(total) as a window, ordered by date and id.
Use ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW.

title: The order before
statement: Return order id, customer_id, ordered_at and that customer's previous order date. Exclude guest orders (NULL customer_id), include all statuses. Previous means ordered_at ascending, then order id ascending; a customer's first previous date is NULL.
solution: SELECT id,customer_id,ordered_at,LAG(ordered_at) OVER(PARTITION BY customer_id ORDER BY ordered_at,id) FROM orders WHERE customer_id IS NOT NULL
hints: LAG reads a previous row in a window.
Partition by customer_id.
Order each window by ordered_at, id.

title: The best of each shelf
statement: Return category_id, product id, name and price for the most expensive product in each non-null category. If prices tie, pick the lowest product id.
solution: WITH ranked AS (SELECT category_id,id,name,price,ROW_NUMBER() OVER(PARTITION BY category_id ORDER BY price DESC,id) AS rn FROM products WHERE category_id IS NOT NULL) SELECT category_id,id,name,price FROM ranked WHERE rn=1
hints: Rank products separately per category.
ROW_NUMBER resolves ties to one row.
Put the rank in a CTE and filter rn = 1 outside it.

title: A slice of inventory
statement: Return category_id, total stock and percentage of all categorised stock rounded to two decimals for each non-null product category. Use 100.0 for percentage arithmetic.
solution: WITH s AS (SELECT category_id,SUM(stock) AS units FROM products WHERE category_id IS NOT NULL GROUP BY category_id) SELECT category_id,units,ROUND(100.0*units/SUM(units) OVER(),2) FROM s
hints: Aggregate stock by category first.
SUM(units) OVER() gives the grand total without collapsing rows.
Divide 100.0 * units by the window total and round.

title: Back for more
statement: Return customer id, name and order count for customers with at least three orders, including all statuses. Exclude guests.
solution: WITH counts AS (SELECT customer_id,COUNT(*) AS n FROM orders GROUP BY customer_id HAVING COUNT(*)>=3) SELECT c.id,c.name,t.n FROM customers c JOIN counts t ON c.id=t.customer_id
hints: Build a CTE of counts by customer.
Keep groups with at least three orders.
Join those counts to customers for their names.

title: Mind the gap
statement: Return employee id, salary and salary minus their department's average salary, rounded to two decimals. Exclude employees without a department.
solution: SELECT id,salary,ROUND(salary-AVG(salary) OVER(PARTITION BY department_id),2) FROM employees WHERE department_id IS NOT NULL
hints: AVG can also be a window function.
Partition by department_id to compute a team average.
Subtract AVG(salary) OVER(...) from salary.

title: Follow the reporting line
statement: Return id, name and depth for Maya Rao (employee id 1) and all her direct or indirect reports. Maya has depth 0; each reporting step adds 1.
solution: WITH RECURSIVE team(id,name,depth) AS (SELECT id,name,0 FROM employees WHERE id=1 UNION ALL SELECT e.id,e.name,t.depth+1 FROM employees e JOIN team t ON e.manager_id=t.id) SELECT id,name,depth FROM team
hints: Use a recursive CTE with Maya as the anchor.
Join employees.manager_id to the current team id.
UNION ALL adds reports with depth + 1.

title: One row, the whole story
statement: Return customer_id, delivered-order count and cancelled-order count for every customer_id appearing in orders (excluding NULL). Include customers with zero in either count. Do not include customers with no orders.
solution: SELECT customer_id,SUM(CASE WHEN status='delivered' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END),SUM(CASE WHEN status='cancelled' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) FROM orders WHERE customer_id IS NOT NULL GROUP BY customer_id
hints: Conditional aggregation makes a compact pivot.
CASE can return 1 for a status and 0 otherwise.
SUM each CASE expression, grouped by customer_id.

title: A customer's timeline
statement: Return customer_id, first order date, last order date and whole days between them for every non-null customer_id with orders. Include all statuses.
solution: WITH dates AS (SELECT customer_id,MIN(ordered_at) AS first_date,MAX(ordered_at) AS last_date FROM orders WHERE customer_id IS NOT NULL GROUP BY customer_id) SELECT customer_id,first_date,last_date,CAST(julianday(last_date)-julianday(first_date) AS INTEGER) FROM dates
hints: Find MIN and MAX order dates per customer.
Use a CTE to give those dates readable names.
Subtract julianday(first_date) from julianday(last_date).

title: What really brings it in?
statement: Return product id, name and delivered-order net revenue rounded to two decimals for products sold in delivered orders. Sort revenue descending, then product id ascending. Net value is quantity × unit_price × (1 − discount).
solution: SELECT p.id,p.name,ROUND(SUM(i.quantity*i.unit_price*(1-i.discount)),2) AS revenue FROM products p JOIN order_items i ON i.product_id=p.id JOIN orders o ON o.id=i.order_id WHERE o.status='delivered' GROUP BY p.id,p.name ORDER BY revenue DESC,p.id
hints: Join products, items and orders.
Filter delivered orders and group by product.
Sort by the rounded revenue descending and id ascending.

title: Short and sweet
statement: Return customer id, name and the character length of name for customers whose full name has fewer than 9 characters, counting spaces.
solution: SELECT id,name,LENGTH(name) FROM customers WHERE LENGTH(name)<9
hints: SQLite LENGTH counts text characters.
Use the function in both SELECT and WHERE.
Compare LENGTH(name) < 9; spaces count too.
